title: CI/CD and trunk-based development
subtitle: Merge small changes every day, let a machine build and test each one, and ship the same tested build to production.

c.v: On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital's trading system sent millions of orders it should not have sent. In about 45 minutes it got over 4 million executions (filled trades) in 154 stocks. Knight lost over $460 million.

The cause was a deploy. Starting on 27 July, Knight put new code on its eight order-routing servers, a few at a time. A technician did not copy the new code to one of the eight. No second technician reviewed the deploy, and no written procedure asked for one.

The new code reused an old flag. On seven servers the flag turned on the new feature. On the eighth, it woke up old code called Power Peg, unused since 2003. A 2005 change had broken how that code counted filled shares. So it never knew an order was filled, and kept sending more.
It got worse. While trying to fix it, the team removed the new code from the seven good servers. Now those servers ran the old code too.
The SEC report is about missing controls, not about

tools. But the pattern is common. A manual, step-by-step deploy means each server can end up different. In our view, an automated pipeline that ships one build to every server, and checks the version, makes this mistake much harder.
Everyone merges small changes into one shared branch, often. Fowler suggests every developer commits to the mainline every day.
Each merge is built and tested by a machine. If the build breaks, you fix it right away.
Your software can be released to production at any time. Deploying any version is one button press.
One step further. Every change that passes the pipeline goes to production with no human step. With continuous delivery you are able to deploy often, but you may choose not to.

Small changes, merged often, each one built and tested by a machine. Small changes are easy to review, easy to test and easy to undo.
Step through one commit, from trunk to users. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.

When a branch lives for weeks, everyone else keeps changing trunk too. At the end, you face a long merge with many conflicts. Fowler calls the worst case "integration hell": every integration bug you fix shows two more.
Short-lived feature branches avoid this. A branch should live a couple of days at most, with one developer, or two when pairing. You open a
, CI runs, a teammate reviews, you merge and delete the branch.

"Only build packages once" is one of the core pipeline practices. You want to be sure the thing you deploy is the thing you tested.
Deploy it the same way to every environment.
Knight's servers ran different code. With one artifact, promoted everywhere, that is much less likely.
A red build on trunk blocks everyone. If the commit stage fails, fix it at once, and nobody adds new work on top.
Often the fastest fix is to revert your change, then fix it calmly on a branch.
GitHub can enforce part of this. With required status checks, nobody can merge into a protected branch until the checks pass.
Google's CI chapter says the cost of a bug grows almost exponentially the later you catch it. So CI aims for fast feedback.
Google runs only fast, reliable tests before submit. Slower tests run after submit.
Fowler says a ten-minute build is reasonable.

DORA studies software delivery. Its guide now names five
time from a commit in version control to that change running in production.
how many deploys you do in a period, or the time between them.
how long it takes to recover from a deploy that fails and needs immediate action.
the share of deploys that need immediate action after they go out.

Note that recovery time counts as throughput here, not instability.
DORA says speed and stability are not trade-offs. For most teams the metrics are correlated.

Your pipeline can run code from strangers, so it is also an attack path. GitHub advises pinning third-party actions to a full-length commit SHA. A tag can be moved or deleted by someone who gets access to that repository.

The author of GitFlow wrote in 2020 that web apps are usually delivered continuously. For them he suggests a simpler flow. GitFlow still fits when you must support several versions in use at once.
start with trunk-based development and continuous delivery. Move to continuous deployment once your tests and rollback are trusted.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Keep pull requests small. If a PR is open for more than two days, ask how to split it.
Ask "can we ship this unfinished, behind a flag?" before anyone creates a long-lived branch.
Treat a red main branch as an urgent problem for the whole team. Revert first, debug second.
Watch the CI time. When it grows past about ten minutes, move slow tests out of the merge check or run them in parallel.
with an owner and a date. Never make "just re-run it" the normal fix.
Check that production runs the exact artifact that passed tests. Ask: "Can anyone deploy a build that did not go through the pipeline?"
Track change lead time and change fail rate together. Use them to find slow or risky steps, not to rank people.
Remove dead code and old flags. Knight's old code stayed callable for years.

now open pull requests on their own. On GitHub, Copilot's cloud agent can push to only one branch. By default, CI does not run on its pull request until a person with write access approves the workflow run. The person who asked the agent cannot approve its pull request.
In our view, CI becomes the main safety net for agent code. It runs on every change and does not get tired.
"Here is our CI workflow. Find steps that are slow or run in series but could run in parallel. Estimate the time saved for each."
"List every third-party action and dependency in this repo that is not pinned to an exact version or commit SHA. Propose the pinned versions."
"This feature is too big for one PR. Split the plan into PRs of under 200 lines. Each must keep main green, with new behaviour behind a flag that is off."
The agent's tests test real behaviour. A test with no real assertion is always green.
The pull request does not change the CI workflow, skip tests or loosen checks without a clear reason.
New dependencies are real, well-known packages at pinned versions.
The agent did not "fix" a red build by deleting or disabling a failing test.

q.v: Your team's pipeline tests every merge and puts each passing build into production with no human step. What is this called?

why.v: In continuous deployment every change that passes the pipeline goes to production on its own. Continuous delivery means you could deploy at any time, but a person chooses when.

q.v: A feature will take three weeks. How do you keep working on trunk?

options.v: Keep one branch for three weeks and merge it at the end.
Merge small parts every day, with the unfinished feature behind a flag that is off.
Work in a fork and copy the files over when done.

why.v: Small daily merges keep conflicts small. The flag keeps unfinished work hidden from users.

q.v: Why should the pipeline build the artifact once and promote it, instead of building again for production?

options.v: It saves a little disk space.
So the thing you deploy is exactly the thing you tested.
Because production servers cannot run a compiler.

why.v: A new build can pick up different dependencies or settings. Promoting one build means your tests are about the real release.

q.v: Which pair are both DORA throughput metrics?

options.v: Change lead time and deployment frequency.
Change fail rate and deployment rework rate.

why.v: DORA groups change lead time, deployment frequency and failed deployment recovery time as throughput. Change fail rate and rework rate measure instability.

q.v: An AI agent opens a pull request. Its tests all pass. What is still your job?

options.v: Nothing. Green CI means the change is correct.
Read the diff, check that the tests test the right thing, and look for changes to the pipeline itself.
Re-run CI three times to be sure.

why.v: CI only checks what its tests check. An agent can write weak tests or change the workflow files, so a human still reviews.
